documents.unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: CETL Syllabus Template (includes Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence section)
documents.stance_why: The Policy box says "Every instructor may determine for their own class what uses of generative artificial intelligence are permissible", and the template then supplies two sample options (permitted with or without limitations; not permitted). It sets no university-wide stance and hands the choice to instructors, so it delegates.
tiers: Generative AI permitted (with or without limitations)
documents.summary: CETL's syllabus template contains a Use of Generative AI section. It states that each instructor decides acceptable AI use, advises clear communication, transparency and assessment changes because bans are hard to enforce and detectors unreliable, and gives sample permitted and not-permitted syllabus language.

units.why: The Policy box says "Every instructor may determine for their own class" what AI uses are permissible, so the rule is set per instructor. Actor is instructor, phase before-course (policy design); P04 rather than P85 because the decision sits with instructors, not units.
units.anchor: Every instructor may determine for their own class what uses of generative artificial intelligence are

units.why: The same sentence ties instructor-set rules to the "Academic Conduct and Discipline Policy" and says instructors decide which uses "constitute academic dishonesty", so improper AI use is handled as misconduct; P36 fits.
units.anchor: what uses constitute academic dishonesty as outlined in the Academic Conduct and Discipline Policy
units.fit_note: Instructors decide which uses count as dishonesty; the type assumes misuse is already defined.

units.why: "Instructors should be as clear as possible in their syllabi" asks instructors to state AI expectations in the syllabus and in class; a communication duty, P09.

units.fit_note: Also asks instructors to speak with their classes, beyond the syllabus.

units.why: "generative AI may serve as a learning tool or as an obstacle" says AI can help or hinder course goals. It sets no rule but links the instructor choice to course goals; P83 fits best.
units.anchor: generative AI may serve as a learning tool or as an obstacle in helping students
units.fit_note: Frames AI as a tool or obstacle relative to course goals; does not require the decision to follow stated learning objectives.

units.why: The template offers suggested language for "a range of attitudes toward AI use" and two named options (permitted, not permitted); named categories of use, P05.

units.why: "outright bans on generative AI are increasingly difficult to enforce" admits that bans cannot be fully enforced; P82 fits.

units.why: "student misuse of AI may be undetectable and unprovable" is a distinct claim about limits on proof, one of the three stated reasons; P82 fits.

units.why: "students may not always know when they are using AI" is a separate premise that students cannot always tell whether a tool uses AI; nearest P103, though it concerns tool opacity.

units.why: "We recommend, therefore, that instructors clearly communicate about what constitutes (un)acceptable AI use" recommends explicit communication of acceptable use; P09.
units.anchor: instructors clearly communicate about what constitutes (un)acceptable AI use

units.why: "encourage transparency around AI use" recommends that instructors encourage openness about AI use, i.e. disclosure; P24 fits though it is only encouraged, not required.

units.why: "make modifications to their assessments that would prevent or discourage AI misuse" recommends redesigning assessment around AI, P35.
units.anchor: make modifications to their assessments that would prevent or discourage AI misuse

units.why: "grading schemes that reduce stress and enhance student motivation (and that address the root causes of academic dishonesty)" recommends prevention by easing pressures; P99 rather than P35, which is about AI-proofing assessment.

units.why: The "Not Permitted" template says "I ask that you refrain from employing AI tools in this course", a course-level ban phrased as a request; P01 despite the softened phrasing.

units.why: "skills that are important to practice on your own" gives the reason for the ban: AI may inhibit skill development, so it shortcuts practice (P41).
units.anchor: we’ll be developing skills that are important to practice on your own

units.why: "will violate our academic integrity policy" classes use of AI in the not-permitted course as an integrity violation, P36.

units.why: "it may not always be clear whether or not you are interacting with AI within these applications" is the instructor acknowledging, in the not-permitted option, that embedded AI is hard to spot; P07.

units.why: The course-policy list says "Instructors may also wish to include the following optional policies", and the AI statement is on that optional list, so the template does not require an AI syllabus statement. P09 is the nearest type.

units.why: "the language for each policy is only suggested" lets instructors alter the AI sample language to their course, supporting instructor-level control (P04).
